sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
An overdetermined linear equation \(Ax \approx b\) usually has no exact solution. Least squares asks for the \(x\) that makes the residual \(Ax - b\) as small as possible in the Euclidean norm. The objective \(\lVert Ax - b\rVert^2\) is a quadratic in \(x\). Its gradient is \(2 A^T(Ax - b)\), and its Hessian is \(2 A^T A\).

Setting the gradient to zero produces the normal equations \(A^T A x = A^T b\). The same equation says the residual is orthogonal to every column of \(A\). That is the geometric picture: the residual is perpendicular to the column space, so \(Ax\) is the orthogonal projection of \(b\) onto that subspace.

The Hessian is positive definite exactly when \(A\) has full column rank. Then \(A^T A\) is invertible and the minimizer is unique, \(x = (A^T A)^{-1} A^T b\). If the columns are dependent, \(A^T A\) is singular. The normal equations stay consistent, because \(A^T b\) lies in the column space of \(A^T A\), but the solution is no longer unique. Every solution has the same residual.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The normal equations and the full-column-rank solution are
\[
A^T A x = A^T b, \qquad x = (A^T A)^{-1} A^T b.
\]
For one column \((p, q)\) and a right-hand side \((u, v)\), the scalar unknown is \((p u + q v)/(p^2 + q^2)\). The residual of the fitted vector is orthogonal to the columns.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Four measurements of one unknown are \(1, 9, 3, 11\), and the column is a column of ones. The normal equation is \(4x = 24\).

The gauge mean is 6. The residual is \((-5, 3, -3, 5)\), and it sums to zero, which is orthogonality against the single column of ones. The squared residual is \(25 + 9 + 9 + 25 = 68\). The fit is unique because a nonzero column has full column rank. It is not an exact fit, and least squares does not pretend that it is.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Replacing \(A^T b\) by \(b\) is the algebra error that breaks the shapes. The right-hand side has to live in the column space of \(A^T\). A second error is to declare \(A^T A\) invertible just because \(A\) is tall. Tall matrices can have repeated columns. A third is to use the full-row-rank formula \((AA^T)^{-1}\) on a tall full-column-rank matrix. That Gram matrix is the large one, and it is singular. A fourth is to expect a zero residual. A zero residual means \(b\) was already in the column space. The normal equations do not require that.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A line or a polynomial is linear least squares once the unknowns are the coefficients and the columns are powers of the input. A residual that depends nonlinearly on the parameters is no longer a single normal equation. Its Jacobian plays the role of \(A\) at the current parameters, and a step of that kind is how later methods move. A recursive update of the same normal equation, one block of rows at a time, is the least-squares form of a linear filter.
